faq.q1: Do I need an account to browse?
faq.a1: No. Vendors, tips and schedule examples are open without registration. You only need an account when you want to save a vendor or create your own plan.
faq.q2: We don't have a date yet — can I still start?
faq.a2: Yes. Date, city and budget can be skipped — “not decided yet” is a complete answer. The plan adapts once you fill in the details later.
faq.q3: How do I contact a vendor?
faq.a3: From the vendor's profile — see packages, starting price and portfolio, then check date availability. A saved vendor is not automatically booked.
faq.q4: Can I plan together with my partner?
faq.a4: Yes. Grant your partner access from settings and you both work on the same plan.
faq.q5: I already found a photographer elsewhere.
faq.a5: Add them manually under “My vendors” — with price and payment dates. Not every vendor has to be on the platform.

trust.finalNote: Browse without registering. An account only when you want to save or create a plan.

landing.heroTitle: Your wedding guest list, finally in one place
landing.heroSubtitle: Add everyone you’re inviting, keep plus-ones and children straight, and see your real headcount at a glance — on your phone or laptop.
landing.heroNote: Free for couples. No spreadsheet skills needed.
landing.feature1Title: Add by hand or upload a spreadsheet
landing.feature1Text: Type guests in one at a time, or bring the list you already have as a CSV file. Either way, every name lands in the same table.
landing.feature2Text: Mark who brings a partner or kids. The tool totals adults and children separately, so the number you give the venue is the one you actually seat.
landing.feature3Text: Tag each guest as “definitely” or “maybe” invited. When the venue or budget sets a limit, you see both headcounts instantly and decide without starting over.
landing.tipsTitle: How to build a wedding guest list
landing.tipsText: A few things that make the list easier, especially for Georgian weddings.
landing.tip1Text: In Georgia the parents’ circle is often half the room. Ask both sides for their list early, and enter them under “family” so you can see who comes from where.
landing.tip2Text: Venues and caterers charge per seat. A family of four is four plates — add partners and children as separate guests from the start.
landing.tip3Text: Some guests won’t be able to come. A ready B-list lets you send a second round of invitations without the stress of deciding under pressure.
landing.nextSeatingText: Once the list is set, drag your guests onto tables and see who sits where.
landing.nextBudgetText: Your headcount drives most of the cost. Check what it means for your budget.
landing.faq1q: How many guests does a Georgian wedding usually have?
landing.faq1a: It varies a lot. Traditional weddings often bring together a few hundred people, while city weddings are increasingly held for 80–150. Start from your venue’s capacity and your budget per seat, then build the list to fit.
landing.faq2q: Who should go on the list first?
landing.faq2a: Close family and the wedding party, then the parents’ closest relatives and friends, then your own friends and colleagues. Doing it in that order makes the inevitable trimming far easier.
landing.faq3q: How do we handle plus-ones and children?
landing.faq3a: Decide one rule and apply it to everyone — for example, plus-ones for guests in long-term relationships, and children of close family only. The tool tracks partners and children as separate guests so the headcount stays honest.
landing.faq4q: When does the guest list need to be final?
landing.faq4a: Venues usually ask for a final number two to three weeks before the wedding. Send invitations well before that, and keep your “maybe” list ready in case someone declines.
landing.faq5a: Yes. Create a free couple account, and your list is saved to it — open it on any device, share it with your partner, and it stays in sync.
landing.finalText: It takes a minute to sign up, and your list grows with you from the first name to the final count.

landing.heroTitle: A seating chart you drag, not draw
landing.heroSubtitle: Add your venue’s tables, drop guests onto seats, and see at a glance who still needs a place — no paper, no eraser.
landing.heroNote: Free for couples. Works with your guest list.
landing.feature1Text: Round or long, 6 seats or 12 — add the tables you’ll actually have and arrange them on the canvas the way the room is laid out.
landing.feature2Title: Drag guests straight from your list
landing.feature2Text: Everyone on your guest list appears in a side panel. Drag a name onto a seat; plus-ones and children come along.
landing.feature3Text: A running count shows seated versus total, so an empty chair or a forgotten cousin never makes it to the wedding day.
landing.tipsText: A few rules of thumb that keep the room happy.
landing.tip1Text: Parents, grandparents and the wedding party take the tables nearest the couple. Fill those first, and everyone else falls into place.
landing.tip2Title: Mix by circle, not by family
landing.tip2Text: A table of people who already know each other is safe; a table where each guest knows at least one other person is lively. Aim for the second.
landing.tip3Text: Someone always brings an unexpected guest. One or two spare seats near the back save you from re-shuffling on the day.
landing.nextGuestsText: Seating starts with the list. Add names, plus-ones and children, then come back here.
landing.nextBudgetText: Every table has a price. See what your headcount means for the venue and catering lines.
landing.faq1q: When should we make the seating chart?
landing.faq1a: Once the guest list is close to final, usually two to three weeks before the wedding. Earlier than that you’ll redo it; later, and the venue won’t have time to set the tables.
landing.faq2q: Do Georgian weddings use assigned seats?
landing.faq2a: Increasingly yes, at least by table. Large supras still often seat by family side, and the tamada’s table is fixed. Assigning tables rather than individual chairs is the usual compromise.
landing.faq3q: Where do the couple and parents sit?
landing.faq3a: The couple take the head table, with the parents and the wedding party either at the same table or the two closest ones. Everyone else radiates outward from there.
landing.faq4q: What about divorced parents, or guests who don’t get along?
landing.faq4a: Give each their own table with their own people, at equal distance from the couple. The chart makes it easy to try a layout, look at it, and move a table before anyone sees it.
landing.faq5q: Can we use the chart at the venue?
landing.faq5a: Yes — open it on your phone at the venue walk-through or on the day. Each table lists exactly who sits there, so place cards and the caterer’s plan match what you decided.
landing.finalText: Sign up free, build your guest list, and the seating chart is ready when you are.

landing.feature1Text: Type one number and get a recommended split across venue, catering, photo, dress and more, based on how Georgian weddings actually spend.
landing.feature2Text: After you sign up, each line tracks three numbers — so you always know what’s promised, what it really cost, and what’s still owed.
landing.feature3Text: Link a photographer or venue from the directory straight to its budget line, and set a reminder for the next payment date.
landing.tipsTitle: How to budget for a wedding
landing.tipsText: The habits that keep the number from drifting.
landing.tip1Text: Venue and catering are priced per seat and usually make up more than half the total. Fix the guest count first and the rest of the budget follows.
landing.tip2Text: Something always comes up: a second dress fitting, extra transport, a bigger cake. A line you don’t allocate at the start is the cheapest insurance.
landing.tip3Text: Deposits are paid months apart and easy to forget. Record each one against its line the day you pay it, and the final week has no surprises.
landing.nextGuestsText: The headcount behind every number here. Build the list and the budget gets real.
landing.nextSeatingText: Once the venue line is settled, arrange the tables you’re paying for.
landing.faq1q: How much does a wedding in Georgia cost?
landing.faq1a: There is no single number: a restaurant wedding for 150 and a vineyard wedding for 60 can cost the same. The split above is the useful part — it shows where the money usually goes, whatever the total.
landing.faq2a: The venue and the table: hall rental, food and drink per guest. Photo and video come next, then the dress, decor and music.
landing.faq3a: Traditions vary by family and region, and many couples now split costs with both sets of parents. Agree it early and enter each contribution as part of the total, so nobody is surprised later.
landing.faq4q: Can I change the recommended split?
landing.faq4a: Yes — every amount is editable, and the remaining figure updates as you type. The recommendation is only a starting point.
landing.faq5a: Yes. The estimate above is free without an account, and the full tracker is free with a couple account. The number you enter here carries over when you sign up.
landing.finalTitle: Turn the estimate into a real budget
landing.finalText: Sign up free and keep the number you just entered — every line becomes trackable.
